source_title: San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance — giraffe
facts: Giraffes have seven neck bones, the same number as humans.
A giraffe's spotted coat is individually distinctive, rather like a fingerprint.
Giraffe horns are skin-covered structures called ossicones, and both sexes have them.
Giraffes can move both legs on one side forward together when walking.
A giraffe's tongue can reach around acacia thorns to gather leaves.
Giraffes chew cud and have four stomach compartments.
A newborn giraffe drops to the ground because its mother gives birth standing up.
Giraffe calves can stand and walk within about an hour of birth.
Giraffe mothers sometimes form nurseries, with one adult watching while others feed.
Giraffes are not silent: they can snort, grunt, hiss, and make other sounds.

source_title: San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance — elephant
facts: An elephant's trunk has no bones or cartilage.
Elephants suck water into their trunks, then pour it into their mouths to drink.
Elephant tusks are enlarged incisor teeth.
New elephant molars move forward from the back of the jaw like a conveyor belt.
An elephant's large ears help release heat from its blood.
Wrinkles in elephant skin trap moisture and help the animal stay cool.
Some elephant calls are too low-pitched for human ears.
Elephants can favour one tusk, much as people favour one hand.
Elephant herds can form a protective circle with calves in the middle.
An elephant pregnancy can last around 22 months.

source_title: San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance — hippo
facts: A hippo's reddish skin secretion is neither blood nor ordinary sweat.
Hippos produce a skin coating that helps protect them from sunburn.
Hippos can surface for air while sleeping without fully waking.
Hippos move underwater by pushing off the bottom rather than paddling like dogs.
A hippo's eyes, ears, and nostrils sit high enough to work while most of it is submerged.
Hippos can close their nostrils underwater.
A hippo's wide-open mouth can be a threat display rather than a sleepy yawn.
Hippos usually leave the water after sunset to graze on land.
Hippo mothers can nurse their calves underwater.
Hippos use their tails to scatter dung when marking territory.

source_title: San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance — okapi
facts: The zebra-striped okapi is a giraffe relative, not a kind of zebra.
Okapis have oily coats that help shed rainforest water.
Scent glands on okapi feet leave a trail that other okapis can smell.
Okapis make some calls at frequencies too low for humans to hear.
An okapi's large ears help it detect danger in dense forest.
An okapi's flexible tongue strips leaves and buds from vegetation.
Okapi calves hide in secluded places while their mothers forage.
Newborn okapis can stand within about half an hour.
Okapis sometimes eat clay, probably to obtain minerals.
Forest communities knew okapis long before scientists formally described them in 1901.

source_title: San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance — platypus
facts: A platypus finds underwater prey partly by detecting its electrical signals.
A swimming platypus closes its eyes and ears while hunting.
The platypus bill is flexible and soft, unlike the hard bill of a duck.
Platypuses carry caught food in cheek pouches before eating at the surface.
A platypus stores energy as fat in its tail.
Adult platypuses grind food with tough mouth pads instead of teeth.
Young platypuses lose their temporary teeth before adulthood.
Male platypuses are among the few mammals equipped to deliver venom.
A platypus is a mammal that lays eggs and then feeds its young milk.
Platypus fur traps insulating air that helps keep the animal warm in cold water.

source_title: San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance — echidna
facts: A baby echidna is called a puggle.
An echidna mother carries her egg in a temporary belly pouch.
Newly hatched echidnas have no projecting spines, making the pouch a gentler home.
Echidna mothers secrete milk without having nipples.
Echidnas grind food against hard mouth pads because they have no teeth.
An echidna's backwards-pointing hind feet help it groom between its spines.
Echidnas can dig down until only their protected, spiny backs remain exposed.
An echidna's snout can detect electrical signals from its prey.
Echidnas can swim despite their squat appearance.
Echidna mothers move their young into burrows as the youngsters develop spines.
